passage: I'm Rajni, and I sat behind a little boy called Nitin on the bus to town. He looked out of the window and asked his mother, "Why is the sky blue? Why is that cow brown? Why does the road go on?" She didn't know the sky one. She said, "Good question. I'll ask your uncle, he studied science." About the cow she said, "That's how she was born." Nitin nodded, satisfied, and asked the next one. I couldn't tell how much he understood, but he kept asking, and she kept turning to listen.

qa.q: What three questions did Nitin ask on the bus?
qa.a: Nitin asked why the sky is blue, why that cow is brown and why the road goes on.

qa.q: What was Nitin probably feeling as he kept asking?
qa.a: Nitin seemed curious and content, nodding when answered and moving on to the next question. Rajni cannot be sure how much he understood.

qa.q: What did Nitin's mother do that made the questions feel welcome?
qa.a: She said it was a good question, admitted she did not know the sky answer, promised to ask his uncle and kept turning to listen.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mother have felt about the stream of questions on the bus?
qa.a: She was probably a little stretched but kind, since she kept turning to listen and answering honestly.

grounding: A child asks endless why questions; an adult who treats them as worth answering matters more than the answers.

passage: Monday: Five-year-old Ganga asked her father, Omkar, why the moon kept coming along with the car. He slowed down. "Good question. What do you think?" Wednesday: he brought a library book about the moon and looked at the pictures with her. Saturday: Ganga sat with Nani and explained, "The moon is very far, so it seems to follow us!" Nani asked, "Who taught you that?" Ganga said, "We looked it up. I asked."

qa.q: What did Ganga ask her father on Monday?
qa.a: Ganga asked why the moon kept coming along with the car.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling on Saturday as she explained about the moon?
qa.a: Ganga was proud and excited to share what she had found out.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that kept Ganga's curiosity going?
qa.a: Omkar said it was a good question, asked what Ganga thought and then brought a library book to look at together.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt hearing Ganga explain the moon?
qa.a: Nani was probably surprised and pleased, since Nani asked who taught it and heard that Ganga had asked and looked it up.

grounding: A child asks about the moon and the car; an adult treats the question as worth answering across several days.
